sections.html:
North Carolina takes part of a qualifying owner's home value off the tax rolls. For the elderly or disabled exclusion, the amount removed is the larger of two figures: a fixed $25,000, or one half of the county's appraised value of the residence.

The state runs three owner-relief programs, and one form covers them all. Form AV-9 goes to your county tax assessor, since the Department of Revenue does not take it. An owner can draw on only one program at a time, so pick the one that saves the most.

sections.h2: Who qualifies for the elderly or disabled exclusion?
sections.html:
Three things must be true on the January 1 before the tax year: you live in North Carolina, you are at least 65 or totally and permanently disabled, and your prior-year income was at or under the cap. The rule is in Chapter 105, section 277.1 of the General Statutes.

  • The 2026 form sets the income cap at $38,800, up from $37,900 for 2025. It follows the Social Security cost-of-living percentage.
  • Every kind of income counts, with one carve-out: gifts or inheritances that came from a spouse, parent, grandparent or descendant. Spouses who share a home combine their incomes.
  • A protected residence is the dwelling plus its lot up to one acre and related improvements. Houses, apartments in multi-family buildings and manufactured homes all fit.
  • The disability needs certification from a physician who practices in this state or from a government agency.
  • A couple gets the whole exclusion even if only one spouse meets the test.

This one takes $45,000 off the appraised figure, and the state's own form says it has no age or income limit. Its statute is section 277.1C.

The owner must live in North Carolina, hold an honorable or under-honorable-conditions discharge, and either draw benefits under 38 U.S.C. 2101 or hold a VA certification of permanent and total service-connected disability. An unmarried surviving spouse can claim it too. Begin with a county veteran service officer, who helps complete Form NCDVA-9. Then file it at the assessor's office.

The circuit breaker caps the tax bill at a share of household income and postpones the rest. Owners at or under the cap pay no more than 4.0% of income. Owners above it but within 150% of it pay no more than 5.0%.

The 2026 form puts those two thresholds at $38,800 and $58,200. Applicants must be at least 65 or have a total and permanent disability, live in this state, and have owned and occupied the house as their permanent residence for five years. You file every year, not once.

The postponed tax becomes a lien. If something disqualifies the owner, such as a transfer, a death or a move out, the deferred taxes for the previous three fiscal years become payable.

The place to file Form AV-9 is the county tax assessor, and the time is the January listing window. It opens on the first working day of the year and closes January 31. Late applications are still taken through the first of June.

One form serves all three programs, so ask the assessor whether you meet more than one test. Each year brings a new income cap, so pick up the form for the tax year you are claiming.

sections.h2: What to bring to the assessor
sections.html:
Each county handles intake itself, so ask the assessor's office for its checklist before you go. Most files need the same evidence.

  • Proof of age, or the certificate of permanent and total disability.
  • Prior-year income records for the owner and for a spouse in the same home.
  • Proof the property is the owner's permanent residence, with acreage if the lot exceeds one acre.
  • For the circuit breaker, evidence of five years of ownership and occupancy.
  • For the veteran exclusion, the VA certification or benefits record and a completed Form NCDVA-9.

Arriving with every paper at the first visit saves a return trip and keeps you inside the January window. Make copies, and ask for a dated receipt when you hand the form in.

sections.h2: How the income cap changes each year
sections.html:
The state resets the number annually with the Social Security cost-of-living percentage. The 2026 form shows $38,800 against $37,900 for 2025, and its $58,200 upper circuit breaker line equals 150% of the 2026 cap.

An owner just over the line one year can land under it the next, so one denial does not decide later years. Circuit breaker relief ends unless you reapply annually. Ask the assessor whether your county wants repeat filings for the other two programs.

sections.h2: Can you also appeal the appraised value?
sections.html:
Yes, and the appraisal matters because every program here is measured against it. In most counties the commissioners act as the review board. Its first meeting comes in spring, somewhere between early April and early May.

Request a hearing, by letter or in person, before the board wraps up its work. A decision is mailed within 30 days after adjournment. An owner who still disagrees can give written notice to the Property Tax Commission within 30 days after that mailing. The elderly or disabled version takes the bigger of a flat figure and half the value, so a lower appraisal can change which side of that comparison controls. Call your assessor for the county's own appeal calendar and forms.

sections.h2: Selling a home that receives this relief
sections.html:
A sale is a transfer, and a transfer is one of the events that makes deferred circuit breaker tax payable. Get a written payoff figure from the county tax collector ahead of closing, so the title agent can pay it from your proceeds.

  • The seller also pays deed excise tax at the register's office before the deed is filed. The rate is one dollar for every five hundred of price, with any partial five hundred counted.
  • Each year's bill is due September 1, and anything unpaid picks up 2% interest on January 6.
  • Heirs who inherit from a circuit breaker owner may face the deferred bill too, because the owner's death is a triggering event.

Deferred tax is a lien, so clear it with the collector rather than leaving the buyer to find it. If you already receive any of the three benefits, tell your closing agent at the outset so the payoff request reaches the county early. A cash sale with a flexible closing date gives you time to sort out the payoff without a lender's deadline pressing on you.

faqs.q: How large is the North Carolina homestead exclusion?
faqs.a: The elderly or disabled version cuts the bigger of $25,000 and half the appraisal. The disabled veteran version removes a flat $45,000.
It is $38,800 for 2026. For 2025 the limit was $37,900.

faqs.q: Where do I file the application?
faqs.a: File with your county tax assessor on Form AV-9. A disabled veteran first completes Form NCDVA-9 with a county veteran service officer.

faqs.q: Can I get more than one program?
faqs.a: No. The three programs are alternatives, and an owner draws on one of them.

faqs.q: What if I miss the January 31 filing date?
faqs.a: You still have time. Assessors must accept applications until June 1 of the tax year.
